Actuarial statistics uses probability theory and statistical inference to quantify insurance claims, premiums, and the uncertainty of future losses. Aggregate claims model describes portfolios, reinsurance redistributes losses, and the Bühlmann model combines experience with population information.

No claims discount system

Words: 612 Articles: 6
Actuarial statistics OurBigBook.com
A policyholder's future insurance premiums depend on a finite discount level, updated according to whether a claim is submitted in each year. With independent yearly accidents and repair costs, and a claim decision depending only on the current level and cost, the level is a discrete-time Markov chain. Accident probability and submitted-claim probability differ when the policyholder pays small repair costs without claiming.

Two-year no-claims threshold with reset to zero (a0​=βC,aα​=aβ​=(2β−α)C)

Words: 84
No claims discount system OurBigBook.com
In a no claims discount system with discounts 0,α,β, a reported claim resets next year's discount to zero. With no later accidents, the next two premiums after reporting are C+(1−α)C. At the zero level, not reporting instead gives (1−α)C+(1−β)C; at either other level it gives 2(1−β)C. Their differences give the displayed repair-cost thresholds. A fully reimbursed loss above its threshold should be reported under this undiscounted two-year rule. Current premiums cancel. Different thresholds generally produce state-dependent submitted-claim probabilities, even with a common accident mechanism.

Persistent claim intensity can destroy the discount Markov property

Words: 118
No claims discount system OurBigBook.com
Let a policyholder have one fixed exponential distribution intensity Λ of rate ν, with conditionally independent annual Poisson distribution counts. Its one-year marginal count is geometric, but averaging that count does not make the discount process a Markov chain. In the three-level rule, start at zero discount. At time three, the histories 0,α,β,β and 0,0,α,β both end at the same top level. The first means three no-claim years, giving next no-claim probability (ν+3)/(ν+4). The second means a positive count followed by two zero counts, giving (ν+2)/(ν+4): divide the integrals of (1−e−λ)e−(ν+3)λ and (1−e−λ)e−(ν+2)λ. These are distinct, so the Markov property fails when only the current discount is recorded. Conditioning on the intensity, or recording its Bayesian posterior, restores the required predictive information.

Three-level discount equilibrium with geometric annual counts (π=1−p2q(q2(1+p),pq,p2)​,p+q=1)

Words: 87
No claims discount system OurBigBook.com
Suppose annual claim counts are independent with geometric distribution mass pqj, j≥0. In a no claims discount system with discounts 0,α,β, a claim returns either of the first two levels to zero; at the top, one claim sends the level to α and two or more send it to zero. The transition matrix is (qqq2​p0pq​0pp​). Solving πP=π gives the displayed stationary distribution. With full premium c, the stationary expected value of the premium is c[1−(αpq+βp2)/(1−p2q)]. Independent annual sampling is essential; a persistent random intensity does not justify this marginal transition matrix.

Three-level no claims discount equilibrium (π∝(p2​p3​,(1−p1​)p3​,(1−p1​)(1−p2​)))

Words: 51
No claims discount system OurBigBook.com
For a three-level birth-death chain whose down-or-stay claim probabilities are p1​,p2​,p3​, with each in (0,1), detailed balance is π1​(1−p1​)=π2​p2​ and π2​(1−p2​)=π3​p3​. Normalizing gives the displayed stationary distribution. The finite chain is irreducible and has endpoint holding probabilities, so it is aperiodic and its level proportions converge to this distribution from any initial level.

Two-year premium-loss claim threshold (b∑r=12​(dir0​​−dir1​​))

Words: 211 Articles: 1
No claims discount system OurBigBook.com
Let b be the undiscounted annual premium and di​ the discount fraction at level i. Compare the next two levels ir0​ after no current claim with ir1​ after a current claim, assuming no later accidents. Their total additional premium is the displayed threshold. A repair cost above it makes a claim advantageous under this two-year rule. For discounts 0,α,β and one-level moves with reflecting endpoints, the thresholds at levels one, two, and three are respectively bβ, b(2β−α), and b(β−α). The premium scale must be specified or fixed as the monetary unit.

Incremental second-claim threshold at the highest discount level (L1​>c(β−α),L2​>cβ)

Words: 116
Two-year premium-loss claim threshold OurBigBook.com
For a no claims discount system with discounts 0,α,β, assume a policyholder starts at β, the first claim lowers next year's discount to α, and a second claim in the same year lowers it to zero. With no further losses and undiscounted future premiums, claiming for the first loss costs c(β−α) in extra premium. Once that claim is submitted, the second claim adds cα next year and c(β−α) the year after, a total cβ. Thus the second decision uses the incremental threshold, not the cost of both claims relative to no claim. For independent unit-rate exponential distribution losses the probabilities are e−c(β−α) and e−cβ, respectively; the latter remains the conditional probability given submission of the first claim.

Expected value premium principle (Π(L)=(1+θ)EL)

Words: 52
Actuarial statistics OurBigBook.com
The expected value principle prices a nonnegative insurance loss L by its expected value times one plus a positive loading. In the classical risk model, annual expected claim cost λμ gives premium rate (1+θ)λμ. Under quota share reinsurance, the reinsurer prices its ceded fraction (1−α)S using its own loading, which need not equal the direct insurer's loading.

Credibility estimate (μ​=ZX+(1−Z)μ)

Words: 339 Articles: 5
Actuarial statistics OurBigBook.com
A credibility estimate combines a risk's individual experience with population information. In the basic equal-exposure form, the credibility factor Z weights the observed sample mean, while 1−Z weights a prior or collective expected value. The Bühlmann credibility premium is the best affine estimate under mean squared error; an exact Bayesian posterior mean can also have this form, as in the natural conjugate credibility identity.

Bayesian credibility

Words: 291 Articles: 4
Credibility estimate OurBigBook.com
Bayesian credibility estimates a risk's conditional mean by its Bayesian posterior expected value under squared-error loss. When that posterior mean is an affine combination of exposure-weighted individual experience and a prior mean, the coefficient of the experience is its credibility factor. Exact Bayesian credibility is distinct from merely selecting the best affine estimator when the true posterior mean is nonlinear.

Normal-normal credibility (θ=ZX+(1−Z)μ,Z=nσ22​/(σ12​+nσ22​))

Words: 103 Articles: 1
Bayesian credibility OurBigBook.com
Conditionally independent normal distribution observations of mean θ and known variance σ12​, with normal prior mean μ and variance σ22​, give normal-normal conjugacy with known observation variance. Their posterior mean has the displayed exact credibility estimate form. It minimizes posterior squared-error loss and predicts the conditional mean of the next observation.
Normal-normal credibility with unequal exposures (Z=Wσ2/(v+Wσ2),W=∑j​mj​)
Words: 63
Normal-normal credibility OurBigBook.com
For conditionally independent annual averages Xj​∣θ∼N(θ,v/mj​) and prior θ∼N(μ,σ2), the posterior mean is ZXw​+(1−Z)μ, with Xw​=∑j​mj​Xj​/W. Completing the quadratic likelihood gives posterior precision σ−2+W/v. This is an exact Bayesian credibility version of the Bühlmann–Straub credibility estimate. Increasing the between-risk prior variance increases the experience weight; increasing process variance decreases it. The next total pure premium is mn+1​ times the estimated per-life mean.

Inflation-adjusted Poisson-gamma credibility (Yn+1​=cn+1​β+∑j​wj​α+∑j​wj​yj​/cj​​)

Words: 71
Bayesian credibility OurBigBook.com
For a common gamma distribution (shape α, rate β) frequency prior distribution and conditionally independent Poisson distribution yearly counts of means wj​Θ, observed average amounts yj​ determine counts kj​=wj​yj​/cj​. The posterior distribution shape is α+∑j​kj​ and rate is β+∑j​wj​. The future per-policy mean is the display, equal to credibility factor W/(W+β) times ∑j​(wj​/W)(cn+1​/cj​)yj​ plus the complementary weight times cn+1​α/β. The data must lie on their count lattice; impossible noninteger recovered counts have zero likelihood.

Exact beta-binomial credibility with unequal exposures (Z=M/(M+α+β))

Words: 61
Bayesian credibility OurBigBook.com
For a common success chance with beta prior and conditionally independent binomial observations of sizes mi​, put M=∑i​mi​ and s=∑i​xi​. Beta-binomial conjugacy gives posterior mean (α+s)/(α+β+M), equal to Z(s/M)+(1−Z)α/(α+β). Multiplying by the next exposure predicts its expected count. The factor tends to one as exposure increases and to zero as prior concentration increases at fixed prior mean.

Bühlmann model (m=E[m(Θ)], v=E[v(Θ)], a=Var(m(Θ)))

Words: 605 Articles: 12
Actuarial statistics OurBigBook.com
Given a latent risk parameter Θ, observations are independent and identically distributed random variables with conditional expectation m(Θ) and conditional variance v(Θ). The Bühlmann credibility premium estimates m(Θ) by an affine function of past observations under mean squared error. Its population parameters are m=Em(Θ), expected process variance v=Ev(Θ), and variance of hypothetical means a=Var(m(Θ)).

Bühlmann–Straub model (Var(Xj​∣Θ)=σ2(Θ)/mj​)

Words: 187 Articles: 3
Bühlmann model OurBigBook.com
Conditional on a common latent variable Θ, annual averages Xj​ are independent, have common conditional expectation μ(Θ), and have conditional variance σ2(Θ)/mj​ for known positive exposures mj​. Its structural parameters are m0​=Eμ(Θ), expected process variance v=Eσ2(Θ) and variance of hypothetical means a=Var(μ(Θ)). It generalizes the equal-exposure Bühlmann model.

Bühlmann–Straub credibility estimate (μ​=ZXw​+(1−Z)m0​)

Words: 146 Articles: 2
Bühlmann–Straub model OurBigBook.com
For total exposure W=∑j​mj​ and weighted average Xw​=∑j​mj​Xj​/W, the best affine mean squared error estimate of the conditional mean is ZXw​+(1−Z)m0​, where Z=Wa/(Wa+v). If the coefficients sum to B, their error is a(1−B)2+v∑j​bj2​/mj​. Cauchy-Schwarz inequality minimizes the latter term at bj​=Bmj​/W, and a one-dimensional quadratic minimization then gives B=Z.

Bühlmann–Straub credibility estimate OurBigBook.com
With a Poisson-gamma conjugacy with unequal exposures model, m0​=v=α/β and a=α/β2, so the Bühlmann–Straub credibility factor is W/(W+β). The credibility estimate simplifies to (α+∑j​Yj​)/(β+W), exactly the posterior mean and hence the Bayes estimator under squared error loss. Bühlmann–Straub credibility factor (Z=Wa+vWa​)
Words: 52
Bühlmann–Straub credibility estimate OurBigBook.com
The experience weight is Z=Wa/(Wa+v), where W is total observed exposure, a the variance of hypothetical means, and v the expected process variance. With positive a, it is W/(W+v/a). More exposure raises the weight; larger process noise lowers it. If a=0, the unknown conditional mean is constant and one can set Z=0.

Bühlmann credibility premium (m=ZX+(1−Z)m)

Words: 278 Articles: 4
Bühlmann model OurBigBook.com
The Bühlmann credibility premium is the best affine mean squared error estimate of a risk’s conditional claim expected value. In the Bühlmann model it is ZX+(1−Z)m, where Z=na/(na+v). The linear least-squares projection equations use Var(Xj​)=a+v and Cov(Xi​,Xj​)=a for distinct years.

Balanced-panel method-of-moments credibility (a=max(0,B−v/n),Z=na/(na+v))

Words: 88
Bühlmann credibility premium OurBigBook.com
For independent comparable risks observed over n≥2 years, estimate the expected process variance v by the average within-risk sample variance. The sample variance B of the risk means estimates a+v/n, where a is the variance of hypothetical means. Thus B−v/n is unbiased for a; truncating at zero produces a practical nonnegative estimate but introduces bias. Use the grand mean for m and plug these estimates into the Bühlmann credibility premium ZXs​+(1−Z)m. At least two risks are needed for B; a single year cannot estimate within-risk variance this way.

Poisson credibility with a shape-three Pareto intensity (m=(k+3)/(n+2))

Words: 75
Bühlmann credibility premium OurBigBook.com
Let a fixed policy intensity have prior density 3θ−4 on θ>1, and let n annual claim counts be conditionally independent with Poisson distribution mean θ. The expected process variance is 3/2 and the variance of hypothetical means is 3/4, so the Bühlmann credibility factor is n/(n+2). A total count k gives the displayed credibility premium. By contrast, the Bayesian posterior density is proportional to θk−4e−nθ on θ>1. Its mean is the ratio ∫1∞​θk−3e−nθdθ/∫1∞​θk−4e−nθdθ. For n=2,k=5, that Bayesian credibility estimate is 5/3, whereas the affine estimate is 2.

Bühlmann credibility for inverse-gamma observations (Z=n(k−2)+α+1n(k−2)​)

Words: 39
Bühlmann credibility premium OurBigBook.com
In the Gamma prior for an inverse-gamma scale model, assume k>2. The variance of hypothetical means is a=α/[λ2(k−1)2], and the expected process variance is v=α(α+1)/[λ2(k−1)2(k−2)]. The Bühlmann credibility factor is Z=n/(n+v/a), giving the displayed expression. The optimal affine credibility estimate is (1−Z)α/[λ(k−1)]+ZX. Its fixed-weight arithmetic-mean form differs from the reciprocal-based posterior mean.

Sequential Bühlmann credibility update (mn+1​=mn​+(xn+1​−mn​)/(n+1+K))

Words: 42
Bühlmann credibility premium OurBigBook.com
With fixed structural parameters and K=v/a, the Bühlmann credibility estimate has form (∑i=1n​xi​+Km0​)/(n+K). The next observation updates it by the displayed rule. Consequently the estimate decreases exactly when the new observation is less than the previous credibility estimate, with strict equality handled separately.

Credibility factor (Z=na/(na+v))

Words: 34
Bühlmann model OurBigBook.com
The credibility factor in the Bühlmann model is the weight Z=na/(na+v) placed on the sample mean after n observations. The remaining weight is placed on the population expected value. More experience or larger variance of hypothetical means increases Z; larger expected process variance decreases it.

Variance of hypothetical means (a=Var(E[X∣Θ]))

Words: 37
Bühlmann model OurBigBook.com
The variance of hypothetical means in the Bühlmann model is the between-risk variance of the conditional claim expected value. It creates the shared covariance a between different years of the same risk and determines how much individual experience should influence the premium.

Expected process variance (v=E[Var(X∣Θ)])

Words: 30
Bühlmann model OurBigBook.com
The expected process variance in the Bühlmann model averages within-risk conditional variance over the population of risks. It measures variation that repeated observations can average out and contributes v/n to the variance of the sample mean.

Classical risk model (Ut​=u+ct−∑j=1Nt​​Xj​)

Words: 2k Articles: 32
Actuarial statistics OurBigBook.com
The classical risk model has surplus Ut​=u+ct−∑j=1Nt​​Xj​, where Nt​ is a Poisson process of rate λ, independent claim sizes are positive, and premiums flow in at constant rate c. The relative safety loading is ρ=c/(λEX1​)−1. Ruin is the first time surplus becomes negative.

Finite-claim ruin probability (ψn​(u)=P(min1≤j≤n​UTj​​<0))

Words: 92
Classical risk model OurBigBook.com
In a classical risk model, Tj​ is the time of the jth claim. The displayed probability restricts ruin to the first n claims and increases to the ultimate ruin probability. Conditioning on the first arrival and severity gives ψn+1​(u)=E[FX​(u+cT1​)+∫0u+cT1​​ψn​(u+cT1​−x)fX​(x)dx], with ψ0​=0. For exponential distribution claims of mean μ and relative safety loading ρ, put d=1+ρ and h=d+1. Then ψ1​(u)=e−u/μ/h and ψ2​(u)=e−u/μ(h−1+(u/μ)h−2+dh−3). The recursion follows because a surviving first claim leaves fresh independent future arrivals and claims. The formulas follow by integrating the rate-λ first-arrival density; the claim-arrival rate cancels with c=dλμ.

Maximum aggregate loss in a classical risk model (L=supt≥0​(S(t)−ct),P(L>u)=ψ(u))

Words: 60
Classical risk model OurBigBook.com
Starting from capital u, ruin occurs exactly when the aggregate loss exceeds u. Positive relative safety loading and the strong law of large numbers make S(t)−ct tend to minus infinity, so its supremum is finite almost surely. For exponential distribution claims of rate α, L has an atom 1−λ/(αc) at zero, and, conditional on L>0, has exponential distribution of rate α−λ/c. The ultimate ruin probability determines this mixture directly.

For a nonnegative claim size X of finite positive mean μ, its equilibrium claim-size distribution has this density and survival function FI​(x)=μ−1∫x∞​FX​(t)dt. The tail integral formula for moments normalizes the density. Its moment-generating function is (MX​(r)−1)/(μr) wherever finite, so at an adjustment coefficient it equals one plus the safety loading.

Equilibrium claim-size distribution OurBigBook.com
A nonnegative lifetime or claim law is new better than used in expectation if its mean residual life at every age with positive survival is at most its original mean. The displayed equivalent inequality says that its equilibrium claim-size distribution is no larger in stochastic order than the original law. For an Erlang distribution of shape two and rate one, the two survival functions are (1+x/2)e−x and (1+x)e−x, so the condition holds.

Classical risk model OurBigBook.com
The probability that the insurance surplus in a classical risk model becomes negative at some finite time, starting from capital u≥0. Ultimate survival has probability 1−ψ(u). A finite-horizon ruin probability instead restricts the crossing time to a specified time interval.

Ultimate ruin with exponential claims (ψ(u)=αcλ​e−(α−λ/c)u)

Words: 47
Ultimate ruin probability OurBigBook.com
For rate-α exponential distribution claims and c>λ/α, the ruin integro-differential equation reduces to ψ′′+(α−λ/c)ψ′=0. Differentiate the convolution and use its equation A′=αψ−αA to eliminate it. Positive relative safety loading implies ψ(u)→0 as u→∞, and the zero-capital survival probability gives ψ(0)=λ/(αc). These two conditions determine the displayed solution. The adjustment coefficient is α−λ/c.

Ultimate ruin probability OurBigBook.com
In the classical risk model, condition on the first arrival of the Poisson process. If available capital just before it is v, ruin has probability FX​(v)+∫0v​fX​(x)ψ(v−x)dx. Integrate this expression at v=u+ct against λe−λt and change variables from t to v. Differentiating the lower limit gives the displayed equation. The claim-density convolution is continuous for bounded ψ, so the first-arrival representation also supplies the differentiability required by the equation.

Ruin integro-differential equation OurBigBook.com

Applying (D+4)(D+2) to ϕ′=2ϕ−6A4​−A2​ yields ϕ(3)+4ϕ′′+3ϕ′=0. Its solution is fixed by ϕ(∞)=1, ϕ(0)=3/8 and ϕ′(0)=3/4, giving the displayed probability. The derivative condition comes from the original integral equation and excludes spurious solutions of the higher-order equation.

Certain ruin with nonpositive loading and finite claim variance (c≤λμ⟹φ(u)=0)

Words: 97
Classical risk model OurBigBook.com
For positive claims with finite variance and c≤λμ, the classical risk model has ruin probability one from any finite capital. At claim times, surplus increments are independent copies of cT−X with mean c/λ−μ. Negative mean sends their partial sums to minus infinity by the strong law of large numbers. At zero mean, the increments have finite nonzero variance. For every fixed K, the central limit theorem gives limiting probability 1/2 of a partial sum below −K. The probability of unboundedness below is therefore at least 1/2; as a tail event it has probability zero or one by the Kolmogorov zero-one law, and hence one.

A compound mixed Poisson distribution is a random sum of independent claims whose count has a Poisson mixture law: conditional on a nonnegative random intensity Λ, N has Poisson distribution with parameter Λ. The claim sizes are independent and identically distributed random variables, independent of the intensity and count mechanism. If MX​ is their moment-generating function, then MS​(t)=Eexp(Λ(MX​(t)−1)) wherever finite. A gamma distribution intensity of shape r and rate α gives a negative binomial distribution count with shape r and success probability α/(α+1). Independent intensities with common gamma rate add their shapes by additivity of independent gamma distributions with a common rate.

For an independent binomial distribution count N∼Binomial(n,p), the aggregate can also be represented as ∑j=1n​Bj​Xj​, with independent parameter-p Bernoulli random variables Bj​ and independent claim sizes. Its cumulant-generating function is nlog(1−p+pMX​(t)). Its third cumulant is n(pm3​−3p2m1​m2​+2p3m13​) in severity moments. Constant positive claims d give np(1−p)(1−2p)d3, which is negative when p>1/2. Thus positive claim sizes do not by themselves force a positive third central moment.

For independent factories with accident probability p, and independent Poisson distribution claim counts of mean λ per accident, the accident count is binomial and each accident supplies a cluster. The random-sum transform identity gives the displayed probability generating function. In particular the no-claim chance is (1−p+pe−λ)m; a factory with an accident can still have zero claims. The binomial accident law has Panjer parameters a=−p/(1−p) and b=(m+1)p/(1−p).

Take an independent geometric distribution count with P(N=k)=p(1−p)k, k≥0, and sum its independent positive claims. Its moment-generating function is the displayed composition wherever finite. With q=1−p and severity moments mj​, the third cumulant is (q/p)m3​+3(q/p)2m1​m2​+2(q/p)3m13​, which is strictly positive for nonzero positive claims and 0<p<1. The law has an atom of mass p at zero. Its positive-count convention would instead add a factor MX​(t) to the numerator, as in the geometric-sum moment-generating function.

Compound geometric distribution OurBigBook.com
If independent summands have exponential distribution of mean μ and the independent count has a zero-based geometric distribution of parameter p, their random sum of independent claims has an atom p at zero and an exponential positive component of rate p/μ. Its Laplace transform of a nonnegative random variable is p/[1−(1−p)/(1+μs)]=p+(1−p)p/(p+μs). Thus P(S>x)=(1−p)e−px/μ for x>0. Unlike the geometric sum of exponential variables with a positive count, this law is not purely exponential.

For independent rate-λ exponential distribution claims and a zero-based negative binomial distribution count of shape k and parameter p, the random-sum transform identity gives MS​(t)=[p(λ−t)/(pλ−t)]k. This equals the transform of a compound binomial distribution with count Bin(k,1−p) and rate-pλ claim sizes. Conditional on its positive count n, the total has Erlang distribution, whose survival function is the inner exponential-polynomial sum. Conditioning yields the displayed finite mixture distribution formula for x>0. It replaces an infinite mixture and includes the zero-total atom pk through the omitted n=0 term.

For independent and identically distributed random variables Xj​ independent of a nonnegative integer count N, set S=∑j=1N​Xj​, including S=0 when N=0. Conditioning on the count gives E[etS∣N=k]=MX​(t)k, hence the displayed composition of the moment-generating function with the probability generating function. For positive summands the identity holds for all t≤0; positive t requires convergence of the composed series. The chain rule gives κS,1​=a1​b1​, κS,2​=a1​b2​+a2​b12​, and κS,3​=a1​b3​+3a2​b1​b2​+a3​b13​. In raw severity moments mj​=EXj, the third cumulant is a1​m3​+3(a2​−a1​)m1​m2​+(a3​−3a2​+2a1​)m13​. For a geometric distribution count on the positive integers, independent of independent and identically distributed random variables Xi​, the moment-generating function of S=∑i=1N​Xi​ is the displayed expression. Condition on the count and sum a geometric series. For real t, the finite domain requires MX​(t)<∞ and (1−p)MX​(t)<1. Positive summands always permit t≤0, even when no positive exponential moment exists; this gives a Laplace transform of a nonnegative random variable. Geometric sum of shape-two gamma variables (S=dExp(a)+Exp(b))
Words: 64
Geometric-sum moment-generating function OurBigBook.com
Let the summands have gamma distribution with shape two and rate β, and let the independent positive-support geometric distribution count have parameter p. Put a=β(1−1−p​) and b=β(1+1−p​). The aggregate moment-generating function factors as ab/((a−t)(b−t)), so it is the sum of two independent exponential distributions of rates a,b. Its probability density function is ab(e−as−e−bs)/(b−a) for s>0, nonnegative and integrating to one. This contrasts with the geometric sum of exponential variables, which is itself exponential.

The law of a sum of independent identically distributed claims with an independent Poisson distribution count of parameter λ. This is the fixed-time law of a Compound Poisson process.

Compound Poisson distribution OurBigBook.com
If a Poisson distribution count M of clusters has mean ν, and each cluster independently contains a Poisson number of claims of mean λ, then the total count is a compound Poisson distribution with the displayed probability generating function. Conditioning gives EN=νλ and VarN=νλ(1+λ), so it is not Poisson for positive parameters. With independent severities of mean μ and variance σ2, the aggregate payment has mean νλμ and variance ν[λ(σ2+μ2)+λ2μ2]. Independent validity thinning replaces the per-cluster count mean by λ(1−p) and multiplies expected payment by 1−p.

Conditioning on N gives covariance NCov(Y1​,Z1​) and conditional expectations NEY1​,NEZ1​. Law of total covariance and VarN=λ yield the formula. For per-claim excess of loss reinsurance payouts Y=min(X,M) and Z=(X−M)+​, it becomes λME[(X−M)+​]. The insurer and reinsurer aggregates share their claim count and are generally dependent.

If zero-sized claims are allowed, a compound Poisson distribution count parameter need not be unique. Poisson thinning of zero claims gives the displayed positive-claim count parameter and the conditional claim size probability distribution given X>0, without changing the aggregate. If no positive claims occur, the aggregate is identically zero. This matters when representing a finite weighted sum of Poisson distribution counts whose coefficients include zero.

Conditioning on the independent Poisson distribution count in a random sum gives EetS=exp(λ(MX​(t)−1)) wherever finite. Differentiation at zero gives the displayed cumulants when the relevant derivatives exist. The aggregate variance is the count rate times the raw second claim moment, not just the claim variance. Positive moment-generating function arguments need an exponential moment; finite first and second claim moments suffice for the aggregate mean and variance by conditioning or right derivatives at zero of the Laplace transform of a nonnegative random variable.

For a compound Poisson distribution of count parameter λ and severity moments m1​,m2​, the expected value is λm1​ and the variance is λm2​. As λ→∞ with the severity law fixed and m2​<∞, the standardized aggregate converges in distribution to the standard normal distribution. Indeed, the logarithm of its characteristic function is λ[φX​(t/λm2​​)−1]−itλm1​/λm2​​; the second-order expansion of φX​ makes this tend to −t2/2. The approximation loses the zero atom and assigns positive probability to negative losses.

Approximate a compound Poisson distribution of positive claims by a shifted gamma distribution whose first three cumulants agree. Here mj​=EXj are raw severity moments, while the compound cumulants are λmj​. Solve k+α/ν=λm1​, α/ν2=λm2​, and 2α/ν3=λm3​ to obtain the displayed parameters. The approximation captures positive skewness, but not the atom e−λ at zero. Its shift can be negative; with exponential claims of mean μ it is −λμ/3. Matching three cumulants alone supplies no general tail-error bound.

Applying a measurable per-claim retention g to independent claim sizes preserves the compound Poisson distribution form. The transformed severity is the pushforward measure of the original severity law. With count parameter λ, the retained aggregate has expected value λEg(X) and variance λE[g(X)2]. Zero retained marks may be removed by Poisson thinning.

Hurdle decomposition of a positive random sum (L(S)=pδ0​+(1−p)L(S∣S>0))

Words: 62
Random sum of independent claims OurBigBook.com
For positive claim sizes, a random sum of independent claims is zero exactly when its count is zero. Its law is a mixture distribution of a zero atom of mass p=P(N=0) and, with weight 1−p, a random sum whose count has the zero-truncated claim-count distribution. An independent Bernoulli random variable multiplying that positive component gives the same law. This is distinct from arbitrarily inserting additional zeros into an otherwise unchanged count law.

This follows by expanding its moment-generating function as [p+qp/(p−μt)]2.
